## Abstract

Inference of recent population divergence requires fast evolving markers and necessitates to differentiate shared genetic variation caused by ancestral polymorphism and gene flow. Theoretical research shows that the use of compound marker systems integrating linked polymorphisms with different mutational dynamics, such as a microsatellite and its flanking sequences, can improve estimation of population structure and inference of demographic history, especially in the case of complex population dynamics. However, empirical application in natural populations has so far been limited by lack of suitable methods for data collection. A solution comes from the development of sequence-based microsatellite genotyping which we used to study molecular variation at 36 sequenced nuclear microsatellites in seven *Quercus canariensis* and four *Q. faginea* rear-edge populations across Algeria. We aim to decipher their taxonomic relationship, past evolutionary history and recent demographic trajectory. First, we compare the estimation of population genetics parameters and simulation-based inference of demographic history from microsatellite sequence alone, flanking sequence alone or the combination of linked microsatellite and flanking sequence variation. Second, we apply random forest approximate Bayesian computation to identify which of these sequence types is most informative. Whereas analysing microsatellite variation alone indicates recent interspecific gene flow, additional information gained by integrating nucleotide variation in flanking sequences, by reducing homoplasy, suggests ancient interspecific gene flow followed by drift in isolation instead. The weight of each polymorphism in the inference also demonstrates the value of linked variations with contrasted mutation dynamic to improve estimation of both demographic and mutational parameters.

**Subject terms:** Genetic variation, Conservation biology, Biodiversity, Plant ecology, Evolutionary ecology

## Introduction

The build-up of species neutral genetic diversity through time is driven by the balance between recombination, mutation and drift and its spatial distribution structured by dispersal and gene flow. As these processes are tightly linked, understanding of mutational processes can help describe evolutionary processes in play better. This is especially important when studying recently diverged populations or species where the relative contribution of divergence by drift or natural selection, and gene flow, needs to be assessed to predict species evolutionary trajectory. Recent developments of sequence-based microsatellite genotyping (Darby et al. [2016](#CR15); De Barba et al. [2016](#CR5); Vartia et al. [2016](#CR76)) have improved our understanding of molecular variation at microsatellite repeats and in surrounding flanking sequences (Barthe et al. [2012](#CR6); Viruel et al. [2018](#CR77); Lepais et al. [2020](#CR52)). Several studies demonstrated that jointly accounting for linked microsatellite and flanking sequence substitutions provides complementary information from polymorphism evolving at different rates and by different mechanisms (Hey et al. [2004](#CR41); Ramakrishnan and Mountain [2004](#CR71); Payseur and Cutter [2006](#CR64)). Assuming complete linkage due to short physical distance, linked polymorphisms share the same genealogical history. As a result, microhaplotypes combining fast evolving microsatellite repeat variations with the much slower evolving flanking sequence, should provide refined insights about past demographic history with improved estimation of temporal range and resolution (Ramakrishnan and Mountain [2004](#CR71)).

For instance, Hey et al. ([2004](#CR41)) adapted the Isolation with Migration model (IMa) to compound markers, linking flanking sequence haplotype and microsatellite (HapSTR) with an illustration on two Cichlid species who recently diverged with gene flow. Using one such compound marker system improved the inference of the demographic parameters that were difficult to estimate using a single type of marker. They highlighted additional avenues for progress, such as releasing constrains on the stepwise mutation model for the microsatellites and the need to use several independent loci in future applications. Conversely, Ramakrishnan and Mountain ([2004](#CR71)) defined SNPSTR as one or more Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) linked to a microsatellite and demonstrated their use to estimate the timing of recent population divergence using both simulated and real data. They found the divergence time estimated from microsatellite variation on the background of the derived SNP allele to be more accurate and precise that the estimation based on the microsatellite variation alone. Their simulation showed that 20 SNPSTR markers provided a much better estimation that 100 microsatellites, and that the inference was robust to complex demographic scenarios involving gene flow or both population expansions and bottlenecks. In addition, divergence time between African and non-African human populations inferred from microsatellite variation alone was strongly underestimated compared with the estimation based on microsatellite variation linked to the derived SNP alleles (Ramakrishnan and Mountain [2004](#CR71)). In this study, the use of a subset of the data only, i.e. the microsatellite alleles linked to the derived SNP alleles aiming to reduce homoplasy (alleles identical by state but not by descent), led to much better inferences. This clearly illustrates the wealth of information that can be gained from contrasted mutation rates and mechanisms. On a theoretical ground, assuming an island model at migration drift equilibrium, genetic differentiation is related to gene flow by Fst ≈ 1/ (1 + 4Ne.(m + µ)) (Crow and Aoki [1984](#CR13)). As a result, genetic differentiation at equilibrium is expected to be lower for fast-evolving markers (such as microsatellites) compared to slowly-evolving markers (such as SNP). In addition, correlation between genetic diversities estimated at linked markers should also inform about non-equilibrium processes (Payseur and Cutter [2006](#CR64)), with a decrease in correlation following a demographic event such as a bottleneck.

Despite the clear demonstrated potential of using contrasted polymorphisms, these compound marker systems have been rarely studied because their genotyping is challenging (Mountain et al. [2002](#CR61); Šarhanová et al. [2018](#CR74); Barthe et al. [2012](#CR6)). This technical limitation does not hold true anymore thanks to the development of sequence-based microsatellite genotyping that greatly improves the characterisation of microsatellite and linked flanking sequences (Bradbury et al. [2018](#CR9); Viruel et al. [2018](#CR77); Curto et al. [2019](#CR14); Layton et al. [2020](#CR51)). However, now that data from numerous marker systems can be easily collected at population scale, development of statistical approaches that harness this new source of information is needed for meaningful inference (Payseur and Cutter [2006](#CR64)).

Trees are a model of choice to study broad-scale postglacial colonisation patterns following the end of the last glacial maximum (Hewitt [1999](#CR40)). Their unique life history traits, such as long generation time, and the use of uniparentally inherited chloroplast DNA markers, enable the reconstruction of glacial refugia and postglacial recolonization routes (Petit et al. [2002](#CR65)) or even Tertiary geological events (Magri et al. [2007](#CR57)). Nevertheless, studies conducted at a more local scale in regions known to harbour glacial refugia identified fine-scale population genetic structure within refugia (Gómez and Lunt [2007](#CR32)), highlighting the value of more spatially focused studies to understand complex evolutionary processes such as vicariance and secondary contact and gene flow at play within these relict populations throughout the Pleistocene and the Holocene (Rodríguez-Sánchez et al. [2010](#CR73); Feliner [2014](#CR25)). While the Mediterranean basin is a major centre of biodiversity for the European biota, studies remain scarce on the North African side of the Mediterranean basin, which harbours biodiversity hotspots and potential glacial refugia (Médail and Diadema [2009](#CR59); Lepais et al. [2013](#CR54); Feliner [2014](#CR25)). Understanding evolutionary processes in the region is particularly pressing as anthropogenic pressure is rising and increases threats posed by ongoing climate change (Hampe and Petit [2005](#CR35)).

*Quercus canariensis* Willd. and *Q. faginea* Lam. are two oak species that are a good illustration of both the complexity of evolutionary processes that shape present-day biodiversity within species, and the threats faced by rear-edge populations. While the taxonomy of *Q. canariensis* is well defined, the taxonomic status of *Q. faginea* has been debated among taxonomists with two sub-species (*broteroi* and *faginea*) in Algeria, among the four subspecies described in *Q. faginea*, differing by morphological and environmental characteristics (Aissi et al. [2021](#CR2)). The origin of such high level of intraspecific variability is unclear and might involve a combination of genetic drift in isolated populations (Moracho et al. [2016](#CR60)) and interspecific gene flow. Localized at the rear-edge of the distribution range of the species in an area of putative refugia and regional hotspots of biodiversity (Médail and Diadema [2009](#CR59)), these populations are under the direct threat of contemporary environmental changes. A better understanding of the origin of this intra-specific variability and their recent demographic trajectory is paramount to evaluate the evolutionary value and conservation priority status of these populations.

The aim of this study is to assess the value of the joint analysis of microsatellite and flanking sequence variations for population genetic inference in the case of populations or species with a complex history of drift and gene flow. As a proof of concept, we studied molecular variation at 36 sequenced microsatellites across seven *Q. canariensis* and four *Q. faginea* rear-edge populations to decipher their taxonomic status, past evolutionary history and recent demographic trajectory.

Given long pollen dispersal distance, large effective population size and long generation time typical of wind-pollinated tree species such as oaks, we expect high local genetic diversity and low regional genetic structure at neutral nuclear loci. Alternatively, limited pollen dispersal between small remnant forest stands isolated by habitat fragmentation may have led to genetic drift and reduced effective population size, resulting in low local genetic diversity and high regional genetic differentiation typical of relictual populations (Hampe and Petit [2005](#CR35)). These two putative demographic histories can be further confounded by historical or contemporary interspecific gene flow that will additionally blur species limits and contribute to reshuffle genetic diversity across populations.

We first compared patterns of molecular variation and genetic structure observed from different polymorphisms (variation of microsatellite repeat number, SNP in flanking sequence, allele size, all polymorphisms combined as microhaplotype) using genetic diversity and differentiation indices to assess the correlation or complementarity and the resolution power of different polymorphisms. We expect homoplasy within microsatellite loci to blur species limits, but with a weakest effect when accounting for all polymorphisms.

To identify the most likely combination of historical and contemporary processes that shape the current population genetic structure, we used a simulation-based inference approach that is flexible enough to model specific linked-polymorphisms observed at each locus for alternative past demographic scenarios. We derived specific summary statistics, synthetizing population-level molecular variation, that account for linked microsatellite and flanking sequence polymorphisms. We then applied a Random Forest implementation of Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) that retrieves the information content of each summary statistic and of each type of polymorphism to differentiate between concurrent demographic models and to estimate mutation

Heart transplantation is an extremely effective treatment for heart failure that can prolong life expectancy. However, a shortage of donors worldwide is a major drawback, and securing donors is expected to be increasingly challenging in the future (2). For LVAD, destination therapy or bridge-to-transplant is performed; however, complications such as infections and cerebral thrombosis are major problems (3). Although catecholamine treatment and circulatory support could eventually be withdrawn on day 21 after the second attack (Figure 1A), the heart failure persisted (New York Heart Association [NYHA] classification = III). Ultrasonography revealed severe asynergy throughout the wall of the left ventricle (LV) (ejection fraction [EF] = 30%). Positron emission tomography (PET) further revealed ischemia in the middle-apex (anterior wall) and the base-apex (posterior-lateral wall); an infarcted area in the inferior wall was observed despite the absence of significant stenosis in all coronary arteries. # Rewritten Structured Research Report

*Based on:* Miyagawa S, Kainuma S, Kawamura T, Suzuki K, Ito Y, Iseoka H, Ito E, Takeda M, Sasai M, Mochizuki-Oda N, Shimamoto T, Nitta Y, Dohi H, Watabe T, Sakata Y, Toda K, Sawa Y. Case report: Transplantation of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte patches for ischemic cardiomyopathy. *Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine*. 2022;9:950829.

**DOI:** [10.3389/fcvm.2022.950829](https://doi.org/10.3389/fcvm.2022.950829)
**PMID:** [36051285](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36051285/)
**Source (Open Access):** [Frontiers full text](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcvm.2022.950829/full)
**Clinical Trial Registration:** Japan Registry of Clinical Trials, [jRCT2053190081](https://jrct.niph.go.jp/en-latest-detail/jRCT2053190081)

---

## Abstract

Heart failure persists as a condition with high worldwide mortality, exceeding cancer-related deaths among approximately 26 million patients. Allogeneic human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hiPSC-CM) patches, produced under clinical-grade protocols, were investigated as a regenerative approach for ischemic cardiomyopathy. We report a first-in-human case in which three hiPSC-CM patches (3.3 × 10⁷ cells per patch) were implanted onto the left ventricular (LV) epicardium of a 51-year-old male with NYHA class III ischemic cardiomyopathy (baseline LV ejection fraction 30%) via thoracotomy, under intra-aortic balloon pumping (IABP) support and a three-month immunosuppressive regimen. No lethal arrhythmias, tumor formation, or immunosuppression-related serious adverse events were detected over a one-year observation period. NYHA functional class improved from III to II at both 6 months and 1 year. Four-dimensional computed tomography demonstrated enhanced regional wall motion at the grafted sites, while ¹³N-ammonia PET imaging showed that whole-heart coronary flow reserve increased from 2.16 at 6 months to 5.30 at 1 year post-implantation. Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET revealed no evidence of tumorigenesis. These initial findings suggest the procedure was well tolerated and associated with functional recovery, although the single-patient design precludes causal inference.

---

## Introduction

Despite therapeutic advances including pharmacotherapy, left ventricular assist devices (LVADs), and heart transplantation, severe heart failure continues to carry poor prognosis, particularly when a substantial number of functional cardiomyocytes have been lost. While heart transplantation remains the most effective long-term treatment, donor organ shortages represent a persistent global limitation. LVADs are used as destination therapy or bridge-to-transplant, yet carry risks including infection and cerebral thromboembolism. Cell-based regenerative strategies have accordingly attracted considerable interest.

Adult somatic stem cell approaches relying primarily on cytokine-mediated angiogenesis have shown limited efficacy in advanced cardiomyopathy where functional myocyte loss is extensive. An alternative paradigm involves generating cardiomyocytes ex vivo and delivering them to the failing heart with the goal of mechanical and electrical integration. Human iPSCs, capable of differentiating into spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes that also secrete pro-angiogenic cytokines, offer a potential dual mechanism: direct contractile contribution and paracrine support of hibernating myocardium.

The present report describes the first-in-human transplantation of clinical-grade allogeneic hiPSC-CM patches in a patient with chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy who remained symptomatic (NYHA III) despite maximal guideline-directed medical therapy. The intervention was conducted within a formally approved clinical trial protocol (jRCT2053190081) after written informed consent.

---

## Methods

### Case and Baseline Assessment

A 51-year-old male with ischemic cardiomyopathy was enrolled. In 2019, he experienced an acute myocardial infarction treated by percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) targeting all three major coronary arteries. Six months later, a second infarction occurred, complicated by ventricular fibrillation requiring IABP and percutaneous cardiopulmonary support, as well as catecholamine infusion and Impella® support. Circulatory support was withdrawn on day 21 after the second event, but heart failure persisted (NYHA III). Echocardiography demonstrated severe global LV asynergy with an ejection fraction of 30%. PET imaging revealed ischemia in the mid-apical anterior wall and base-apical posterolateral wall, along with an inferior-wall infarct, despite angiographically patent coronary arteries. The patient was maintained on maximally tolerated doses of anti-heart failure medications (beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, digitalis, angiotensin receptor blockers, anti-aldosterone agents, and oral cardiotonic) prior to the procedure.

### hiPSC-CM Patch Production

Allogeneic hiPSC-CM patches were manufactured in the cell processing center at Osaka University Hospital from a clinical-grade master cell bank (MCB) generated at Takara Bio Inc. Clinical-grade iPSCs were procured from the Center for iPS Cell Research and Application (CiRA), Kyoto University. Quality inspections during production assessed viability, cardiomyocyte purity, sterility, mycoplasma, and endotoxin levels. The preparations passed tumorigenicity denial testing as previously described in preclinical studies. No genetic mutations in cancer-associated genes were detected, and in vivo safety was confirmed in severe immunodeficient (NOG) mice.

### Surgical Procedure

Three hiPSC-CM patches, each containing 3.3 × 10⁷ cells, were implanted onto the epicardium of the LV anterior and lateral walls via a left thoracotomy through the fourth intercostal space under IABP support. No adjunctive surgical procedures (e.g., coronary artery bypass grafting) were performed. IABP support was discontinued one day after surgery, and catecholamine infusion was stopped on postoperative day 8. The patient was extubated on postoperative day 1, remained in the intensive care unit for three days (including the day of surgery), and was discharged one month after the procedure with standard rehabilitation.

### Immunosuppression Protocol

A triple immunosuppressive regimen (prednisolone, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil) was administered during the first three postoperative months and then discontinued entirely.

### Outcome Assessment

Cardiac rhythm was monitored continuously via 24-hour ECG and additionally assessed with Holter monitoring at prespecified intervals. Four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT) employing 320 cardiac CT images was used to evaluate regional myocardial displacement and end-systolic wall stress (ESS). Myocardial blood flow (MBF) at rest and under pharmacological stress was measured by ¹³N-ammonia PET at 6 months and 1 year. Tumor surveillance was conducted with fluorodeoxyglucose-PET (FDG-PET). NYHA functional classification, LV end-systolic volume index (LVESVI), and peak oxygen uptake (peak VO₂) were recorded and presented in detail in the original supplementary material.

---

## Results

### Clinical Outcomes and Safety

No postoperative complications, including lethal arrhythmias, tumor formation, or immunosuppression-related severe adverse events, were detected through one year. NYHA functional class improved from III (baseline) to II at both 6 months and 1 year. The specific numerical trajectories of LVESVI and peak VO₂ are provided in Supplementary Table 2 of the original publication; the main text states that LVESVI initially increased after transplantation but had substantially decreased at the one-year assessment, while peak VO₂ improved at both 6-month and one-year time points in the absence of formal cardiac rehabilitation. No anti-heart failure medications were newly introduced or discontinued during the follow-up period.

### Wall Motion and Wall Stress

4DCT analysis showed that the moving distance of the myocardium, particularly in the regions underlying the grafted patches, demonstrated significant improvement at both 6 months and 1 year compared to the preoperative state. End-systolic wall stress was reduced globally and regionally in the transplanted anterior and lateral LV walls at 6 months post-surgery, with some areas showing greater than 20% reduction and others 10–20% reduction on bull's-eye grid analysis.

### Myocardial Blood Flow and Coronary Flow Reserve

At 6 months, resting MBF values by ¹³N-ammonia PET were: left anterior descending (LAD) territory 0.85 mL/g/min, circumflex (Cx) territory 0.69 mL/g/min, and right coronary artery (RCA) territory 0.66 mL/g/min. By one year, resting MBF had slightly declined: LAD 0.65, Cx 0.54, RCA 0.50 mL/g/min.

Under stress, MBF at 6 months was: LAD 1.80, Cx 1.58, RCA 1.49 mL/g/min, improving at 1 year to: LAD 3.19, Cx 2.93, RCA 3.17 mL/g/min.

Correspondingly, whole-heart coronary flow reserve (CFR) increased from 2.16 at 6 months to 5.30 at 1 year. Segmental CFR values showed the following 6-month vs. 1-year changes: LAD 2.12 vs. 4.90; Cx 2.27 vs. 5.40; RCA 2.21 vs. 6.47. The one-year CFR values approached those reported for healthy individuals. LV wall motion at the grafted site showed marked augmentation under stress conditions compared to rest.

### Tumorigenicity Surveillance

FDG-PET imaging at 6 months post-transplantation demonstrated no evidence of tumor formation in the heart or any other organ, consistent with preclinical tumorigenicity testing results.

---

## Discussion

### Key Findings

This first-in-human experience demonstrates that epicardially delivered, clinical-grade allogeneic hiPSC-CM patches were well tolerated in a single patient with advanced ischemic cardiomyopathy and were associated with improvements in functional class, regional wall motion, wall stress, and coronary flow reserve over one year.

### Safety Considerations

Previous work by Shiba et al. (2016) reported increased arrhythmias early after intramyocardial injection of hiPSC-CMs. In contrast, the present case detected no lethal arrhythmias, a finding consistent with the authors' preclinical data showing that the patch delivery method was non-arrhythmogenic. The authors speculate that arrhythmia risk may relate to delivery technique (needle injection vs. epicardial patch), though this hypothesis requires further evaluation.

### Mechanism of Functional Recovery

The mechanism underlying the observed functional improvement remains an open question. Two non-exclusive pathways are recognized: (1) direct cardiomyogenesis, in which transplanted cardiomyocytes electrically couple with the host myocardium and contribute contractile force; and (2) paracrine angiogenesis, in which cytokines released by the graft stimulate perfusion of hibernating myocardium. The observed improvements in CFR, wall motion under stress, and the gradual decline in resting MBF (suggesting more efficient myocardial oxygen utilization at rest) are consistent with the angiogenesis hypothesis. The authors' preclinical study demonstrated new functional vessel formation and implicated the angiopoietin family in vessel maturation.

### Limitations

This study has critical limitations, explicitly stated in the original publication:

1. **Sample size**: A single-patient case report (N = 1) precludes generalization, causal attribution, or statistical inference regarding efficacy.
2. **Graft survival unknown**: Immunosuppression was suspended at three months, and the authors could not determine whether the transplanted hiPSC-CM patches survived in the human heart during the remainder of the observation period.
3. **Mechanistic ambiguity**: The relative contributions of direct cardiomyogenesis versus paracrine/angiogenic effects to functional recovery were not delineated.
4. **Absence of control**: The observational design without a comparator or sham arm limits conclusions about treatment-specific effects.
5. **Short follow-up**: One-year data are insufficient to assess long-term durability, late tumorigenesis risk, or sustained functional benefit.
6. **Generalizability**: The complex manufacturing pathway (clinical-grade iPS cells from CiRA, MCB from Takara Bio, on-site processing at Osaka University) and the requirement for surgical thoracotomy limit scalability and applicability to broader patient populations.

### Future Directions

Areas for further investigation highlighted by the authors include: developing noninvasive methods to track graft cell survival post-transplantation; detailed immunological profiling to optimize immunosuppressive protocols; and co-transplantation with other cell types or tissues to enhance cardiomyogenic efficacy.

### Conclusion

This case report provides initial human evidence that clinical-grade allogeneic hiPSC-CM patch transplantation is feasible and was associated with clinical improvement and no detected serious adverse events through one year in a single patient with ischemic cardiomyopathy refractory to maximal medical therapy. Given the N = 1 design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger controlled studies.

---

## Source Verification Note

All numerical values, clinical details, and limitations in this report are derived from the open-access full text of the original article and its associated supplementary materials (PDF). The precise time-course values for LVESVI and peak VO₂ (presented in Supplementary Table 2 of the original paper) could not be extracted as numerical text because they were embedded as image-based table data within the supplementary PDF; only the qualitative directional descriptions from the main text are reflected here.
